lines.text: The chip in your phone has billions of switches, each smaller than a virus. And it all starts with sand.
Sand is mostly silicon. It's melted and purified until it's ninety-nine point nine nine nine nine nine nine nine percent pure.
A tiny seed crystal is dipped in, and slowly pulled up, growing one giant perfect crystal, called an ingot.
The ingot is sliced into thin shiny discs called wafers, and polished flatter than almost anything on Earth.
Then comes the magic: printing with light. The wafer is coated with a material that changes where light hits it.
The newest machines use extreme ultraviolet light, made by blasting tiny drops of tin with a laser, tens of thousands of times a second.
That light shines through a pattern and shrinks it onto the wafer. Then the exposed parts are etched away.
Coat, expose, etch, repeat. Dozens of layers, stacked like a microscopic city, with copper roads connecting everything.
All of it happens in cleanrooms, thousands of times cleaner than a hospital. One speck of dust can ruin a chip.
Finally, the wafer is tested, cut into hundreds of chips, and each one is sealed in a package.
Billions of switches, working in parallel. That's how Orbi Transfer sends big files too: up to twenty gigabytes, cut into parts, several flying at once.
